name: Piperine (from black pepper)
short: Raises blood levels of medicines: in small human studies, piperine increased levels of phenytoin (in epilepsy patients), carbamazepine, propranolol and theophylline, possibly via absorption or CYP3A4.
text: Piperine's main documented safety issue is that it raises blood levels of other substances taken by mouth. In 20 patients with epilepsy on twice-daily phenytoin, a single 20 mg dose of piperine significantly increased phenytoin blood levels, possibly by increasing absorption, and in six healthy volunteers black pepper soup taken before phenytoin increased its absorption and delayed its elimination; the authors said the significance for patients needs further study. In 12 healthy volunteers, 10 days of piperine increased the peak level, overall exposure and half-life of a single carbamazepine dose by 68.7%, 47.9% and 43.2%, which the authors attributed to inhibition of the enzyme CYP3A4 and for which they advised caution with other drugs metabolised by CYP3A4. In one small crossover study in healthy volunteers (six per drug), piperine increased blood levels of propranolol and theophylline taken by mouth, and in a study in rats and healthy volunteers, 20 mg of piperine increased curcumin bioavailability in the volunteers by 2000%, with no adverse effects reported. A laboratory study showed that piperine inhibits both P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4, which the authors said could affect blood levels of medicines handled by these proteins. A review of piperine in brain and nervous-system diseases noted potential toxicities during long-term use at higher doses and that clinical evidence for that use is barely available. No other adverse effects of piperine itself were described in the cited abstracts.
